source_text: Motus autem animi eius, qui iam per aetatem iudicio rationis uti potest; cui cum poena monstratur et gloria, aut contra commodum vel voluptas, adiutorium et velut occasio offertur, non necessitas imponitur partis alterutrae. Haec igitur voluntas, quae alternatur, originem possibilitatis in libero accepit arbitrio; ipsius vero operis existentiam a se suscipit, nec est prorsus voluntas antequam velit, nec potest velle antequam potuerit et nolle; nec utrumque habet in parte peccati, id est, velle et nolle, antequam usum rationis adipiscitur. Quibus collectis, apparet te verissime definisse: Peccatum est voluntas retinendi vel admittendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere [n48] . Hoc ergo peccatum, quod claruit nihil esse praeter voluntatem, constat genus, id est ipsam originem, ab appetitu proprio suscepisse. Huius species iam in unoquoque, qui dicuntur atomi, reperitur. Differentia vero et in varietate culparum, et in rationibus temporum. Modus est ipsa immoderatio; nam si modus est servire cui debeas, qui hoc praetermittit, veri modi transgressione delinquit. Hic tamen dici subtiliter potest, modum esse peccati, quia nemo plus quam potest delinquit; nam si supra vires, inefficaci voluntate peccatur; hoc ipsum fieri vel sola potuit voluntate. Qualitas autem ascribatur vitio, per quam ostenditur quid amaritudinis, vel dedecore convehat vel dolore. Est ergo peccatum, quia si non esset, nec tu sequereris errores; nihil est autem aliud, praeter voluntatem excedentem ab eo calle, cui debet insistere, et unde liberum est non deflectere. Fit autem de appetitu inconcessorum; et nusquam est nisi in eo homine, qui et habuit voluntatem malam, et potuit non habere.
pass_a_gloss: But it is a movement of the mind of him who already through age can use the judgment of reason; to whom, when penalty is shown and glory, or on the other side advantage or pleasure, help and as it were an occasion is offered, necessity of either part is not imposed. This will therefore, which is alternated, received the origin of possibility in free choice; but the existence of the work itself it takes up from itself, nor is there a will at all before it wills, nor can it will before it could also refuse; nor does it have both in the part of sin, that is, to will and to refuse, before it obtains the use of reason. Which things having been gathered, it appears that you defined most truly: Sin is a will of retaining or admitting what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. This sin therefore, which has become clear to be nothing besides will, stands as having taken its genus, that is its origin itself, from its own appetite. Its species is already found in each one, who are called atoms. But the difference both in the variety of faults and in the reasons of times. The measure is the very immoderation; for if the measure is to serve him whom you ought, he who passes this by offends by transgression of the true measure. Here nevertheless it can be said subtly that there is a measure of sin, because no one offends more than he can; for if above strengths, it is sinned with an ineffective will; this itself could have been done even by will alone. But let quality be ascribed to vice, through which it is shown what of bitterness it conveys either by disgrace or by pain. There is therefore sin, because if it were not, neither would you follow errors; but it is nothing other, besides a will going out from that path on which it ought to insist, and from which it is free not to turn aside. But it is made from appetite of things not conceded; and it is nowhere except in that human who both had an evil will and was able not to have it.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: It is, however, a movement of the mind of someone who is old enough to use rational judgment. When punishment and glory, or on the other side advantage and pleasure, are set before that person, help and, as it were, an opportunity are offered; neither alternative is imposed by necessity. This will, capable of turning either way, received the source of its capacity in free choice. But it brings the actual deed into existence from itself. There is no act of will at all before a person wills, nor can a person will before being capable also of refusing. In the case of sin, a person does not possess both capacities, willing and refusing, before acquiring the use of reason. Taken together, these points show that your definition was entirely true: “Sin is the will to retain or commit something justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain” (Augustine, On Two Souls 15).

This sin, which has been shown to be nothing but will, plainly receives its genus, that is, its very origin, from one's own desire. Its species is then found in each individual, those who are called indivisibles. Its difference lies in the variety of faults and the circumstances of times. Its measure is its very lack of measure. For if the proper measure is to serve the one you ought to serve, whoever neglects this sins by crossing the true limit. Yet one may make the subtle point that sin has a measure because no one sins beyond what he can do. For even if someone sins beyond his powers with an ineffectual will, he was still capable of that very act of willing alone. To vice we must assign a quality through which it shows the bitterness it brings, whether through disgrace or pain. Sin therefore exists; if it did not, you would not pursue your errors. It is nothing other than a will leaving the path on which it ought to remain and from which it is free not to turn aside. It arises from desire for forbidden things, and it exists nowhere except in a person who both had an evil will and could have refrained from having one.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: Indivisibles translates the logical term atomi, meaning individuals, not physical atoms.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
